aiGenerationNote: Produce a 9-minute interactive slide deck. Each slide should introduce a game genre (FPS, RPG, Platformer, Strategy, Adventure) with 2-3 iconic game examples and a brief description of its defining characteristics. Follow this with slides explaining 5-6 core game mechanics (Movement, Combat, Resource Management, Puzzle Solving, Interaction, Progression) using simple animations to illustrate each. screens.title: Exploring Game Genres and Core Mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on two pillars of design: genres, which tell players what to expect, and core mechanics, the verbs that let players act. A genre groups shared conventions like perspective, pacing, and typical challenges — for example, a first-person shooter implies ranged combat from the protagonist's view, while a platformer signals jumping and precision navigation. Core mechanics are distinct: they are the specific rules and interactions, like jumping, shooting, crafting, or leveling. Understanding both helps you design a coherent player experience and choose mechanics that match your audience. As an example, consider how The Legend of Zelda pairs exploration, combat, and puzzle mechanics to create a steady sense of discovery and reward. A common early mistake for designers is polishing art or story while the core mechanic remains unclear; no amount of polish fixes mechanics that don't feel fun. By the end of this lesson you will be able to identify genres by their defining features, name core mechanics in a title you know, and begin sketching simple prototypes that validate one or two core mechanics before expanding the scope.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Exploring Genres & Mechanics

Exploring Game Genres and Core Mechanics

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Learn how categorizing games by genre helps set player expectations, and how core mechanics — the fundamental player actions — shape challenge and fun. You'll see examples and practical ways to prototype mechanics early.

Concept Map
Genre
Labels like FPS, RPG, Platformer
Mechanic
Actions like Jump, Shoot, Craft
Prototype focus
Validate one or two core mechanics before expanding scope.
Explore Key Topics
Genres
Categories like Action, Adventure, RPG and Strategy that set audience expectations.
Core Mechanics
The playable verbs such as movement, combat, and resource management.
Prototyping
Start small: implement one mechanic and test the feel before layering features.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify common video game genres and explain what makes each one distinct. That means recognizing defining features such as perspective, pacing, and typical challenges: for instance, that an FPS centers on ranged combat from the protagonist's view, whereas a platformer centers on jumping and timing. You will also be able to define core game mechanics — the concrete rules and player actions like movement, combat, and resource management — and explain how they shape challenge and fun. Each objective includes a micro-milestone: name three examples for a genre, list three mechanics in a game you know, analyze how a mechanic affects player choices, and sketch a two-mechanic prototype. These skills let you evaluate existing games and make better design decisions early. A useful habit is to play a short session of a title and write down its primary mechanics and how they fit the genre. That simple practice trains your eye to spot good genre-mechanic matches and avoid mismatched combinations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide shows how to practice and verify the skills you are learning. For identifying genres, play short sessions of three different titles and note perspective, pacing, and primary challenges — for example, compare a platformer like Super Mario Bros. with a first-person shooter to see how expectation shifts. To verify you can define mechanics, list three mechanics in a game and describe how the player performs them, such as jumping, reloading, or crafting. For analysis, pick one title and write how a mechanic contributes to fun or frustration — this trains you to link design choices to player experience. For prototyping, implement a minimal loop that contains one mechanic and a simple reward; if players enjoy repeating it, the mechanic has promise. These practice steps are small but meaningful. They turn passive knowledge into a testable skill and help you avoid the common mistake of delaying mechanic validation until late in development.

screens.title: What is a Game Genre?
screens.narratorSegment: A game genre is a practical classification: it groups titles that share conventions, typical mechanics, and a common player expectation. When you say "platformer," players expect precision jumping and level navigation; when you say "RPG," they expect progression and meaningful choices. Genres are not laws: they are useful design shorthand. They help designers pick mechanics, set audience expectations, and create marketing clarity. For example, a First-Person Shooter carries assumptions about camera perspective, combat pacing, and ammunition management. Genres also evolve. Modern titles often blend mechanics from different genres — the key is to understand the defining features so you can combine them intentionally. A common misconception is thinking a game's genre is defined only by story or setting; it's defined by the player's primary actions and the game's systems. To practice, pick three games and list the playable verbs that define their genre. That exercise will show how a single mechanic can move a title towards one genre or another. Consider the difference between a graphic adventure that focuses on puzzles and an action-adventure that layers combat: the presence and weight of mechanics shift the genre label.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › What is a Game Genre?
Definition

A genre groups titles by shared conventions, expected mechanics, and typical player actions.

Why it matters
Genres help define audience expectations and narrow design decisions during early planning.
Common misconception
Setting or story alone doesn't determine genre — mechanics and player actions do.
Example exercise
Play a 15-minute sample and write the game's primary verbs. Label the genre based on those verbs.
Genre Snapshot
Action
Combat, reflexes, platforming. Examples: Super Mario Bros., Street Fighter, Diablo
Adventure
Exploration, puzzles, narrative. Examples: Zork, Monkey Island, The Legend of Zelda
RPG
Progression and choice. Examples: Final Fantasy, The Elder Scrolls, World of Warcraft
Key Takeaway

Genre labels are design tools that arise from the systems and player actions a game emphasizes.

screens.title: Action Games and Their Subgenres
screens.narratorSegment: Action games prioritize physical skill: reflexes, timing, and precise control. Within action you find subgenres that emphasize different verbs. Platformers require jump and movement precision, as in Super Mario Bros., where level design and timing demand mastery of the jump mechanic. Fighting games, like Street Fighter, focus on tight input-to-output mapping and combos — small timing windows create high skill ceilings. Hack and slash titles, such as Diablo, emphasize melee combat against large numbers of enemies and often pair loot systems with quick combat loops. Survival horror shifts the tone by combining limited resources and exploration with vulnerability, making each encounter tense; Resident Evil demonstrates how resource scarcity and restricted movement amplify fear. When designing action systems, think about input responsiveness, feedback, and risk-reward balance. A common pitfall is muddy controls: if movement feels imprecise, platforming and fighting systems break down. A practical test is to prototype a single mechanic — the jump or attack — and measure player ability to reliably perform it. If players struggle, refine input and feedback before adding enemies or levels. Which mechanic would you prototype first for an action title?

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Action Games
Action Subgenres
Platformers
Jumping and navigation precision. Example: Super Mario Bros.
Fighting
One-on-one combat with inputs and combos. Example: Street Fighter
Hack & Slash
Melee combat and loot loops. Example: Diablo
Survival Horror
Resource scarcity and tension. Example: Resident Evil
Design checklist
  • Prototype the core verb (jump, attack) and test for precision.
  • Ensure immediate feedback for successful player inputs.
  • Avoid delayed or floaty controls that undermine skill expression.
Key Takeaway

Action games succeed when core verbs are responsive and provide clear feedback; refine those before adding complexity.

screens.title: Adventure Games and Puzzle Focus
screens.narratorSegment: Adventure games emphasize exploration, narrative, and puzzle-solving rather than reflex-driven combat. Classic text adventures like Zork rely on typed commands and player imagination to solve environmental challenges. Graphic adventures such as Monkey Island shift this to point-and-click interfaces with inventory-based puzzles and dialogue. Action-adventure titles blend exploration with combat and puzzles; The Legend of Zelda is a good example, combining navigation, item-based puzzles, and combat into a single progression loop. Puzzles in adventure games reward observation, pattern recognition, and creative use of items. When designing puzzles, avoid arbitrary solutions that require obscure actions rather than clever reasoning; players should feel rewarded for noticing clues. Another common pitfall is under-signposting: give players subtle hints through environment, NPC dialogue, or item descriptions rather than forcing trial and error. A practical exercise is to design a three-step puzzle where the solution chains items or environmental features. That small design helps you practice chaining mechanics into satisfying discovery moments. How can you make the puzzle feel fair while keeping it challenging? Adventure Games and Puzzle Focus means adventure games prioritize exploration and puzzles; fair clues and item chaining create satisfying solutions.. In practical terms, exploration, narrative, and the role of puzzles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Adventure & Puzzle
Adventure subtypes
Text Adventures — player types commands; example: Zork.
Graphic Adventures — point-and-click inventory puzzles; example: Monkey Island.
Action-Adventure — combines puzzles with combat; example: The Legend of Zelda.
Design guidance
  • Chain puzzle steps logically so each action leads to the next.
  • Provide fair clues via environment and NPC dialogue rather than obscure steps.
  • Test puzzles with fresh players to ensure solutions feel earned, not accidental.
Example task

Design a three-step inventory puzzle that uses one environmental clue and one NPC hint.

screens.title: Role-Playing Games (RPGs)
screens.narratorSegment: Role-Playing Games emphasize character development, narrative choice, and progression systems. RPG mechanics often include gaining experience, leveling up, and unlocking new abilities — these mechanics provide long-term goals and player investment. Subgenres clarify emphasis: JRPGs often present turn-based combat and linear narrative paths, while Western RPGs emphasize open worlds and branching choices. MMORPGs extend progression to persistent worlds with many players interacting. Mechanics in RPGs should support meaningful choices: if leveling only inflates numbers without new options, progression feels hollow. A helpful design rule is to link progression to new decisions or gameplay opportunities, such as unlocking a new ability that enables alternate strategies or access to new areas. Party-based RPGs add composition mechanics where different characters' abilities interact, creating strategic depth. When analyzing an RPG, ask: does each progression step increase player agency or just increase stats? A good progression system rewards both competence and new gameplay possibilities. Try identifying three progression moments in a favorite RPG and note how each one changed what the player could do. Role-Playing Games (RPGs) means rpg progression should unlock new choices or abilities, not only higher numbers.. In practical terms, progression systems, player choice, and party dynamics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Role-Playing Games
RPG subgenres
JRPG — turn-based combat and linear stories. Example: Final Fantasy.
WRPG — player choice and open worlds. Example: The Elder Scrolls.
MMORPG — persistent online progression. Example: World of Warcraft.
Design checklist
  • Make progression unlock new gameplay or choices, not just higher numbers.
  • Balance early and late-game rewards to keep players engaged across progression curves.
  • If using a party, design complementary abilities that encourage experimentation.
Key Takeaway

Progression works best when it expands player agency, creating new meaningful choices.

screens.title: Strategy Games
screens.narratorSegment: Strategy games are defined by planning, resource management, and tactical choices. Real-time strategy (RTS) games like StarCraft require constant decision-making under time pressure: resource gathering, unit production, and positioning all happen simultaneously. Turn-based strategy (TBS) titles such as Civilization let players make careful, discrete decisions and plan long-term strategies across turns. Tower defense games, like Plants vs. Zombies, frame the core loop as building defenses against waves, emphasizing spatial placement and incremental upgrades. Key mechanics include managing limited resources, prioritizing actions, and reading opponent patterns. A common rookie mistake is giving players too many viable resource sinks early on; instead, provide clear trade-offs so decisions matter. When prototyping strategy systems, simulate simple resource loops and opponent behavior to test whether choices feel meaningful. For example, create a mock economy where gathering a resource delays combat upgrades and test whether players make different strategies. The central question for designers is: does the game force trade-offs that make strategy matter? Strategy Games means strategy games succeed when resource trade-offs and tactical choices create meaningful consequences.. In practical terms, planning, resource allocation, and tactical decision-making. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Simulation, Puzzle, Sports, and Racing
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond action, adventure, RPG, and strategy, several other genre families deserve attention because they center on distinct mechanics. Simulation games focus on realistic systems and emergent play — The Sims and Flight Simulator model systems players can manipulate. Puzzle games, such as Tetris or Portal, center on spatial and logical problem-solving and reward pattern recognition. Sports games emulate rules and competitive mechanics found in real-world sports; FIFA uses realistic controls and team tactics. Racing games prioritize vehicle handling, speed management, and track memorization; Mario Kart blends racing with item-based mechanics for chaotic fun. Many modern titles borrow mechanics from these genres, creating hybrid experiences. For example, a racing game can include RPG-like progression for vehicles. When designing or analyzing these genres, ask which system the player spends most time interacting with. If the bulk of playtime is spent customizing and balancing systems, it leans simulation; if the rewarding moment is solving a timed spatial puzzle, it is a puzzle game. That question helps you prioritize which mechanics to prototype and polish first. screens.title: What is a Core Game Mechanic?
screens.narratorSegment: A core game mechanic is a concrete rule or method of interaction that defines how a player engages with a game world. Mechanics are the verbs — jump, shoot, craft, trade, or talk — and they exist at a level below genre labels. For example, movement mechanics determine how an avatar traverses the world: walking, running, jumping, or flying shape the player's sense of mobility. Combat mechanics define how damage, defense, and special abilities work together to create tension and challenge. Resource management mechanics involve gathering, spending, and crafting, which create scarcity and meaningful choices. Puzzle-solving mechanics define how players manipulate objects or recognize patterns. Progression mechanics — experience, leveling, unlocking skills — provide long-term goals. A critical design tip is to choose 1–2 core mechanics to prototype early. That focus helps you measure feel and fun without the distractions of complex systems or narrative. A common mistake is building large content around untested mechanics. Instead, create a minimal loop that isolates the mechanic and observe whether players repeat it voluntarily. That is the clearest test of mechanical fun. What is a Core Game Mechanic? means mechanics are the verbs players use; prototype one or two to test whether a game will be fun.. In practical terms, the actionable rules that define player interaction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Movement Mechanics — Movement as Player Agency
screens.narratorSegment: Movement mechanics determine how players experience space and agency in a game. Walking or running sets baseline pacing; jumping introduces verticality and timing; special movement like flying or teleporting changes traversal entirely. These mechanics influence level design, enemy placement, and challenge. For example, in a platformer the jump's height, hang time, and horizontal control determine which obstacles are solvable and how levels are paced. A useful exercise is to prototype a single movement mechanic and create a short course of obstacles. Adjust parameters like speed or jump height and observe how difficulty and player confidence change. A common designer error is tuning movement in isolation without seeing it in context: movement can feel different when enemies or hazards are present. Also watch for control latency: small delays break the player's trust in the input. To test trust, ask players to perform a precise sequence of moves; if they fail despite correct timing, refine responsiveness. Ultimately movement is a foundational mechanic: when it feels right, everything built on top of it has a chance to shine. Movement properties to tune

Common mistakes
Delayed input or floaty movement that reduces precision.

Try this

screens.title: Combat and Resource Management
screens.narratorSegment: Combat mechanics and resource management often work together to create tension and decision-making. Combat defines how players and enemies exchange actions: attacking, defending, dodging, or using abilities. Resource systems — ammo, health, crafting materials — create scarcity that shapes how often and when players engage. In an FPS, shooting and reloading are core verbs; in survival horror, limited ammo and health force players to choose between confrontation and evasion. Resource management can also be a mechanic in RPGs and strategy games, where collecting and spending materials creates strategic trade-offs. A useful design strategy is to model resource flow early: how quickly players earn a resource and how costly meaningful actions are. If resources are too abundant, choices feel trivial; if too scarce, play may become frustrating. Prototype a simple combat encounter with set resource pools and iterate until players make meaningful choices between using or conserving resources. Watch for a common error: making resources feel arbitrary rather than connected to meaningful decisions. When resources matter, combat becomes strategic, not just mechanical. Combat and Resource Management means link combat and resource systems so scarcity forces meaningful choices rather than arbitrary denial.. Combat mechanics

Example
In a survival encounter, limited ammo makes every shot a strategic choice rather than a reflex.
Resource management
Gathering, spending, and crafting create trade-offs.
Balance income and costs so choices feel meaningful.

Design resources so they encourage strategic behavior rather than gating progress arbitrarily.

screens.title: Blending Genres and Prototyping Mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: Combining genres and mechanics is a powerful route to innovation, but it requires intentional design to avoid producing a disjointed experience. A successful blend identifies complementary mechanics that reinforce a coherent core loop. For example, action-adventure titles like Metroidvania combine platforming and exploration with progression systems that unlock new traversal mechanics, which in turn open earlier areas. Roguelikes combine RPG progression elements with procedural generation and permadeath to create a repeating loop of risk and reward. A common mistake when blending is to place two dominant systems together without creating a bridge — for example, pairing fast, timing-based fighting with slow, menu-driven JRPG progression can feel inconsistent unless you design a unifying mechanic or pacing model. When prototyping blends, isolate the interaction between two mechanics and test their compatibility before expanding content. Build a minimal experience where the two mechanics interact and observe whether players can learn and enjoy both simultaneously. If they cannot, either simplify one mechanic or create a new mechanic that mediates between them. The goal is a harmonious system where combined mechanics create emergent depth instead of friction.

Prototype pattern
Step 1 — Isolate
Implement each mechanic separately to test baseline feel.

Create a tiny scene where the mechanics interact and observe conflicts or synergies.

Adjust parameters or add a mediating mechanic until interaction feels coherent.

When combining fighting and deep narrative progression, consider a mechanic that shortens fights or allows strategic pausing so players can manage narrative choices without being punished for slower decision-making.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the key concepts to remember and use as a quick checklist. Keep these three ideas visible as you analyze or design games: genre frames the promise, mechanics deliver the play, and prototyping reveals what actually works. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on two pillars of design: genres, which tell players what to expect, and core mechanics, the verbs that let players act. A genre groups shared conventions like perspective, pacing, and typical challenges — for example, a first-person shooter implies ranged combat from the protagonist's view, while a platformer signals jumping and precision navigation. Core mechanics are distinct: they are the specific rules and interactions, like jumping, shooting, crafting, or leveling. Understanding both helps you design a coherent player experience and choose mechanics that match your audience. As an example, consider how The Legend of Zelda pairs exploration, combat, and puzzle mechanics to create a steady sense of discovery and reward. A common early mistake for designers is polishing art or story while the core mechanic remains unclear; no amount of polish fixes mechanics that don't feel fun. By the end of this lesson you will be able to identify genres by their defining features, name core mechanics in a title you know, and begin sketching simple prototypes that validate one or two core mechanics before expanding the scope.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify common video game genres and explain what makes each one distinct. That means recognizing defining features such as perspective, pacing, and typical challenges: for instance, that an FPS centers on ranged combat from the protagonist's view, whereas a platformer centers on jumping and timing. You will also be able to define core game mechanics — the concrete rules and player actions like movement, combat, and resource management — and explain how they shape challenge and fun. Each objective includes a micro-milestone: name three examples for a genre, list three mechanics in a game you know, analyze how a mechanic affects player choices, and sketch a two-mechanic prototype. These skills let you evaluate existing games and make better design decisions early. A useful habit is to play a short session of a title and write down its primary mechanics and how they fit the genre. That simple practice trains your eye to spot good genre-mechanic matches and avoid mismatched combinations.

This second objectives slide shows how to practice and verify the skills you are learning. For identifying genres, play short sessions of three different titles and note perspective, pacing, and primary challenges — for example, compare a platformer like Super Mario Bros. with a first-person shooter to see how expectation shifts. To verify you can define mechanics, list three mechanics in a game and describe how the player performs them, such as jumping, reloading, or crafting. For analysis, pick one title and write how a mechanic contributes to fun or frustration — this trains you to link design choices to player experience. For prototyping, implement a minimal loop that contains one mechanic and a simple reward; if players enjoy repeating it, the mechanic has promise. These practice steps are small but meaningful. They turn passive knowledge into a testable skill and help you avoid the common mistake of delaying mechanic validation until late in development.

A game genre is a practical classification: it groups titles that share conventions, typical mechanics, and a common player expectation. When you say "platformer," players expect precision jumping and level navigation; when you say "RPG," they expect progression and meaningful choices. Genres are not laws: they are useful design shorthand. They help designers pick mechanics, set audience expectations, and create marketing clarity. For example, a First-Person Shooter carries assumptions about camera perspective, combat pacing, and ammunition management. Genres also evolve. Modern titles often blend mechanics from different genres — the key is to understand the defining features so you can combine them intentionally. A common misconception is thinking a game's genre is defined only by story or setting; it's defined by the player's primary actions and the game's systems. To practice, pick three games and list the playable verbs that define their genre. That exercise will show how a single mechanic can move a title towards one genre or another. Consider the difference between a graphic adventure that focuses on puzzles and an action-adventure that layers combat: the presence and weight of mechanics shift the genre label.

Action games prioritize physical skill: reflexes, timing, and precise control. Within action you find subgenres that emphasize different verbs. Platformers require jump and movement precision, as in Super Mario Bros., where level design and timing demand mastery of the jump mechanic. Fighting games, like Street Fighter, focus on tight input-to-output mapping and combos — small timing windows create high skill ceilings. Hack and slash titles, such as Diablo, emphasize melee combat against large numbers of enemies and often pair loot systems with quick combat loops. Survival horror shifts the tone by combining limited resources and exploration with vulnerability, making each encounter tense; Resident Evil demonstrates how resource scarcity and restricted movement amplify fear. When designing action systems, think about input responsiveness, feedback, and risk-reward balance. A common pitfall is muddy controls: if movement feels imprecise, platforming and fighting systems break down. A practical test is to prototype a single mechanic — the jump or attack — and measure player ability to reliably perform it. If players struggle, refine input and feedback before adding enemies or levels. Which mechanic would you prototype first for an action title?

Adventure games emphasize exploration, narrative, and puzzle-solving rather than reflex-driven combat. Classic text adventures like Zork rely on typed commands and player imagination to solve environmental challenges. Graphic adventures such as Monkey Island shift this to point-and-click interfaces with inventory-based puzzles and dialogue. Action-adventure titles blend exploration with combat and puzzles; The Legend of Zelda is a good example, combining navigation, item-based puzzles, and combat into a single progression loop. Puzzles in adventure games reward observation, pattern recognition, and creative use of items. When designing puzzles, avoid arbitrary solutions that require obscure actions rather than clever reasoning; players should feel rewarded for noticing clues. Another common pitfall is under-signposting: give players subtle hints through environment, NPC dialogue, or item descriptions rather than forcing trial and error. A practical exercise is to design a three-step puzzle where the solution chains items or environmental features. That small design helps you practice chaining mechanics into satisfying discovery moments. How can you make the puzzle feel fair while keeping it challenging? Adventure Games and Puzzle Focus means adventure games prioritize exploration and puzzles; fair clues and item chaining create satisfying solutions.. Role-Playing Games emphasize character development, narrative choice, and progression systems. RPG mechanics often include gaining experience, leveling up, and unlocking new abilities — these mechanics provide long-term goals and player investment. Subgenres clarify emphasis: JRPGs often present turn-based combat and linear narrative paths, while Western RPGs emphasize open worlds and branching choices. MMORPGs extend progression to persistent worlds with many players interacting. Mechanics in RPGs should support meaningful choices: if leveling only inflates numbers without new options, progression feels hollow. A helpful design rule is to link progression to new decisions or gameplay opportunities, such as unlocking a new ability that enables alternate strategies or access to new areas. Party-based RPGs add composition mechanics where different characters' abilities interact, creating strategic depth. Strategy games are defined by planning, resource management, and tactical choices. Real-time strategy (RTS) games like StarCraft require constant decision-making under time pressure: resource gathering, unit production, and positioning all happen simultaneously. Turn-based strategy (TBS) titles such as Civilization let players make careful, discrete decisions and plan long-term strategies across turns. Tower defense games, like Plants vs. Zombies, frame the core loop as building defenses against waves, emphasizing spatial placement and incremental upgrades.
